commitResults.messageTitle: AGENTS.md: Record project setup and conventions
commitResults.messageBody:
AGENTS.md is the shared context file for AI coding tools working in this repo. Its student profile has [to be filled] placeholders, its JDK note gives a macOS/SDKMAN command, and it says nothing about the commit message conventions the course requires.

An assistant reading it is therefore calibrated to the wrong experience level and toolchain, and has no reason to follow the SE-EDU Git conventions.

Let's:
* record the actual experience level and IDE (VS Code on Linux)
* replace the macOS JDK note with the update-alternatives equivalent
* state the SE-EDU commit message rules and the increment tagging rule

commitResults.messageTitle: Rename chatbot Duke -> Tally
commitResults.messageBody:
The project template names the chatbot Duke, after the Java mascot.
Level-0 requires a distinct name so the product is not confused with
the template or with other students' chatbots.

Let's rename the chatbot to Tally, and rename Duke.java to Tally.java
to match. The name states what the product is for: keeping a tally of
the user's tasks.

The ASCII-art banner, README.md and docs/README.md are updated to
match, leaving no references to the old name.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add greeting and farewell messages
commitResults.messageBody:
Tally prints its banner and exits without addressing the user at all,
so it does not yet read as a chatbot.

Let's greet the user on startup and say goodbye before exiting, with
each message fenced between horizontal rules. The rules keep the
chatbot's output visually separate from what the user types, which
matters once Level-1 adds an input loop.

commitResults.messageTitle: Echo user commands until bye
commitResults.messageBody:
Tally greets the user and exits immediately, so there is no way to
interact with it.

Let's read commands from standard input in a loop, echo each one
back, and exit when the user types "bye". Each message is now fenced
above and below, since the user's typed input sits between messages
and can no longer share a rule with the one before it.

Reading ends on end-of-input as well as on "bye", so that a closed
input stream exits cleanly instead of throwing.

commitResults.messageTitle: Store and list tasks entered by the user
commitResults.messageBody:
Tally echoes each command back and forgets it, so the user cannot
keep track of anything across commands.

Let's store each line the user enters and print the stored lines,
numbered from 1, when the user types "list". An ArrayList holds the
tasks rather than a fixed-size array, so that the collection tracks
its own size and adding or removing tasks later needs no separate
counter kept in step with it.

Listing an empty tally says so explicitly, rather than printing an
empty block that reads as a fault.

Tasks are held in memory only; persistence comes later.

commitResults.messageTitle: Use a Task class to represent tasks
commitResults.messageBody:
Tally stores each task as a bare String, which leaves nowhere to
record anything about a task beyond its description. Marking tasks as
done needs a second piece of state per task.

Let's introduce a Task class holding the description alongside a done
flag, and store Task objects instead of Strings. Task renders itself
through toString, so the listing code no longer has to know how a task
is displayed.

The fields are protected rather than private because Level-4 adds
subclasses for todos, deadlines and events that need to read them.

Listing now shows a checkbox per task and a heading above them, as
Level-3 specifies. Nothing can tick a box yet.

commitResults.messageTitle: Mark tasks as done
commitResults.messageBody:
Tally lists tasks but every checkbox stays empty, so the user has no
way to record that something has been finished.

Let's accept a "mark N" command that ticks the Nth task on the list
and echoes that task back with its checkbox filled, so the user can
see which one changed.

The number the user types counts from 1 while the list is indexed from
0, so the conversion lives in one helper rather than at each command
that names a task.

commitResults.messageTitle: Unmark tasks that are not done after all
commitResults.messageBody:
Marking a task done is irreversible, so a mis-typed task number leaves
the tally permanently wrong.

Let's accept an "unmark N" command that clears the Nth task's checkbox
and echoes the task back, mirroring what "mark" does.

The prefix "unmark " does not collide with "mark ", so the existing
command matching needs no reordering.

commitResults.messageTitle: Use subclasses for the three task types
commitResults.messageBody:
Every task is the same kind of thing, so there is nowhere to record
that one has a due date while another runs between two times.

Let's add Todo, Deadline and Event as subclasses of Task, each
overriding toString to tag itself and to append whatever times it
carries. The tally still holds Task objects, so the listing code
prints any of them without knowing which it has.

Tasks entered without a type keyword become todos, since a bare
description with no date is exactly that. Commands for creating
deadlines and events come next.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add commands for todos, deadlines and events
commitResults.messageBody:
Every task entered becomes a todo, so there is no way to record a due
date, or the times an event runs between.

Let's accept "todo", "deadline ... /by ..." and "event ... /from ...
/to ..." commands, each building the matching task type. Times are
stored as the text the user typed, since Level-4 states that dates
need not be parsed yet.

Adding any task now reports what was recorded and how many tasks the
tally holds, so all three commands confirm identically.

commitResults.messageTitle: Fix task count wording and note AI assistance
commitResults.messageBody:
Adding the first task reports "Now you have 1 tasks in the list",
which reads wrong.

Let's pick the singular or plural noun from the count.

Comments recording where AI contributed are added alongside, per the
course policy on acknowledging AI-generated code.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add automated tests for the console UI
commitResults.messageBody:
Tally's behaviour is only checked by running it by hand and reading the
output, so a change can alter what the chatbot prints without anyone
noticing.

Let's record the expected console sessions in test/ui-test-plan.md and
add a runner that replays each one through the program and compares
what was printed. Expected output is written from the increment
specifications rather than captured from the program, so that a case
can fail rather than merely restate current behaviour.

The runner stops at the first failure and prints the expected output,
the actual output and a diff, since later cases rarely mean much once
an earlier one is broken.

A test-ui skill and a Testing section in AGENTS.md point both Claude
Code and Codex at the runner after each code change.

commitResults.messageTitle: Use exceptions to report what Tally cannot do
commitResults.messageBody:
Bad input either crashes Tally or is silently stored as a task, so the
user is never told what went wrong.

Let's add a TallyException carrying a message written for the user, and
catch it around each command so one bad line reports itself and the
conversation carries on.

Commands are now split into a keyword and its arguments before being
dispatched. Matching on the keyword alone is what lets Tally tell an
unknown command from a known one given nothing to work with, which the
previous prefix matching could not distinguish.

Two errors are handled here: an unrecognised command, and a todo with
no description. The rest follow.

Text with no command word is no longer stored as a todo, so the test
plan case covering that is replaced.

commitResults.messageTitle: Report every bad command instead of crashing
commitResults.messageBody:
Malformed commands still end the program: a deadline with no /by, an
event with no /to, and a task number that is missing, not a number, or
past the end of the list all throw out of main.

Let's check each of them and raise a TallyException naming both the
problem and a command that would work, so the user can correct the
input without guessing at the syntax.

Task numbers are resolved in one place, which is also where the count
from 1 becomes an index from 0, so no command repeats that conversion.

Test cases interleave rejected commands with good ones and list the
tally afterwards, so a bad command that quietly altered the stored
tasks would be caught rather than only its message being checked.

commitResults.messageTitle: Note where AI shaped the command dispatch
commitResults.messageBody:
Record that the switch replacing the if-else chain came from an AI
suggestion, alongside the existing notes in this file, per the course
policy on acknowledging AI contributions.

commitResults.messageTitle: Delete tasks from the tally
commitResults.messageBody:
A task can be added and ticked off but never removed, so anything
entered by mistake stays on the tally for good.

Let's accept a "delete N" command that drops the Nth task and reports
which one went along with the new count. Deleting reuses the lookup
that mark and unmark already share, so a bad number is refused the same
way for all three.

The sentence reporting the count is now shared between adding and
deleting rather than written twice, so the two cannot drift apart.

The list of commands named when Tally does not recognise one is
extended, and the test case checking that message is updated with it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Reject events written with /to before /from
commitResults.messageBody:
Writing an event as "/to ... /from ..." records it with its start and
end times swapped and says nothing about it, leaving the user with a
wrong task that looks right.

Let's split the arguments on /from first, and on /to within what
follows. In that order there is no /to left to find when the markers
are written the wrong way round, so the command is refused instead of
silently reversing the times.

The error now names the required order, and a regression case covering
the swapped input is added to the test plan.

commitResults.messageTitle: Set an explicit serialVersionUID on TallyException
commitResults.messageBody:
Compiling with -Xlint:all warns that TallyException has no
serialVersionUID. Throwable is Serializable, so every exception
inherits that whether the ability is wanted or not, and without an
explicit stamp the JVM computes one from the class's structure.

Let's fix the value at 1, so the warning goes and a later edit to the
class cannot quietly change the stamp.

Tally never writes an exception out as bytes, so this keeps the build
free of warnings rather than protecting any real compatibility.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name the commands with an enum
commitResults.messageBody:
The words Tally accepts are spelled out at each branch of the dispatch
and again in the sentence listing them, so adding a command means
editing two places, and nothing catches it when only one is changed.

Let's name the commands in an enum pairing each with the word the user
types, and build both the dispatch and the list of accepted words from
it. Adding a command now takes one entry, and the sentence offering
the choices follows from it.

Deciding whether a word names a command moves into the enum, so the
dispatch is handed a command it already knows rather than a string it
has to recognise.

commitResults.messageTitle: Save the tally to disk and read it back
commitResults.messageBody:
Every task is lost when Tally exits, so the whole tally has to be
retyped each time the chatbot starts.

Let's write the tasks to data/tally.txt whenever a command changes
them, and read that file back at startup. Each task renders its own
line through toSaveFormat, mirroring the way toString works, so
Storage never has to ask what kind of task it is holding.

The path is assembled from its parts rather than written with a
separator, so it resolves on any operating system, and it is relative
to the project root so the app does not depend on where it sits.

The data file can also be named on the command line. Without that the
tests would share the real tally, and each case would start out
holding whatever the case before it had saved.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refuse to load a damaged data file
commitResults.messageBody:
A data file edited by hand, or truncated by a failed write, can hold a
line that is not in the saved format. Loading what parses and dropping
the rest would leave the user working on a tally that is quietly
incomplete.

Let's name the offending line, say that the tally is starting empty,
and leave the file for the user to fix or delete. Nothing is
overwritten until they type a command, so the file is still there to
repair.

Messages name the file by its file name alone. The full path varies
with where the tally is kept, and the tests would otherwise have to
match a path that changes between machines.

Cases can now seed the data file before a run, which is what lets a
damaged file be tested at all.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-Level-7 into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Brings in saving the tally to disk and reading it back on startup,
together with the handling for a data file that is not in the expected
format.

commitResults.messageTitle: Use American spelling in comments and messages
commitResults.messageBody:
The coding standard the course requires asks for American spelling in
comments, and "recognise" appears both in a Javadoc comment and in the
message shown when the data file cannot be read.

Let's spell both the American way, so the comment complies and the
message beside it does not read differently.

The test case covering that message is updated to match.

commitResults.messageTitle: Move a damaged data file aside before saving
commitResults.messageBody:
Tally refuses to load a data file it cannot read, then destroys it a
moment later: the first command the user types saves the empty tally
straight over it. Even "list" is enough, so the advice to repair the
file cannot be followed.

Let's rename the unusable file to tally.txt.broken as soon as loading
fails, and say where it went. Renaming needs write access to the
directory rather than to the file, so it works even when the file
itself could not be read, and it degrades to the plain message if the
rename fails too.

Cases can now state which files should exist afterwards and what they
should hold. Checking only the console is what let this through, since
Tally printed exactly the right warning while wiping the data.

commitResults.messageTitle: Read deadline dates as dates, not text
commitResults.messageBody:
A deadline keeps whatever text follows /by, so "next Tuesday" and
"2019-10-15" mean equally little to Tally. It cannot tell which
deadline falls first, and can only show a date the way it was typed.

Let's hold the due date as a LocalDate, read from the yyyy-mm-dd form
LocalDate parses without a formatter and shown back as MMM dd yyyy, so
the two forms differ as Level-8 asks. The month name is fixed to
English rather than the machine's locale, so the same tally reads the
same everywhere.

The data file keeps the yyyy-mm-dd form rather than the displayed one,
since that is what LocalDate reads back, so a deadline still survives
a restart.

A date Tally cannot read is refused when typed, naming the form to
use. The same date in the data file is damage instead, because the
user did not type it, so it goes through the path that already sets a
damaged file aside.

Events keep their times as text. Level-8 asks only for deadline dates,
and an event's times are often clock times rather than dates.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-Level-8 into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Brings the deadline due date under java.time, so it is read as
yyyy-mm-dd, shown as MMM dd yyyy, and stored in the form that reads
back.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract a Ui class for talking to the user
commitResults.messageBody:
Tally prints its own messages and reads its own input, so the wording,
the fencing and the command loop are tangled together in one class.

Let's move the greeting, the farewell, the fenced message layout and
the reading of commands into a Ui class. The rest of the code now says
what it means and leaves the laying out to Ui.

Nothing the user sees changes, so the test plan is untouched. The
existing cases are what shows the move was faithful.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract a TaskList class for the tally itself
commitResults.messageBody:
The tasks live in a plain List that Tally passes to every helper, so
each one has to know it is a list and how to work it. Adding a way to
search or sort them later would mean changing all of those signatures.

Let's put the tasks behind a TaskList that offers what the chatbot
actually does to them: add, remove, get, count. Storage still takes a
plain list, since a file holds tasks rather than a tally.

Nothing the user sees changes, so the test plan is untouched.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract a Parser and make Tally an object
commitResults.messageBody:
Tally reads the user's input, decides what each line means, holds the
tasks and prints the replies, so a change to any one of those means
reading past the other three.

Let's move the making sense of a command into a Parser, and turn Tally
into an object holding a Ui, a Storage and a TaskList. Tally now only
decides which of them to call, which is what the switch reads as.

The four classes the increment names are now separate: Ui talks to the
user, Parser reads commands, TaskList holds the tasks, Storage keeps
them on disk.

Nothing the user sees changes, so the test plan is untouched. That the
existing cases still pass is what shows the split was faithful.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-MoreOOP into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Splits the chatbot into the four classes the increment names, so that
each part of the conversation has one place it belongs.

commitResults.messageTitle: Organize the classes into packages
commitResults.messageBody:
Every class sits in the default package, which the coding standard
tells us not to use, and gives no hint of which classes belong
together now that there are eleven of them.

Let's group them by what they are for: tally.ui for talking to the
user, tally.parser for reading commands, tally.task for the tasks
themselves, tally.storage for the file, and tally for the chatbot and
its exception. src/main/java stays the source root, as required.

The test runner now compiles every source under that root rather than
only the files directly in it, and starts tally.Tally rather than a
class with no package.

Nothing the user sees changes, so the test plan is untouched.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-Packages into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Groups the classes into tally.ui, tally.parser, tally.task,
tally.storage and tally, so the default package is no longer used.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge add-gradle-support into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Building and running Tally means naming every source file to javac by
hand, and there is nowhere to declare a dependency such as JUnit.

Let's merge the add-gradle-support branch the course provides, which
brings a Gradle build file and the wrapper. Taking it as given rather
than writing one keeps the build the same as everyone else's, which is
what the grading scripts and the later increments expect.

The build file still names the sample project's main class. Pointing
it at Tally comes next.

commitResults.messageTitle: Point the Gradle build at Tally
commitResults.messageBody:
The build file the course provides names the sample project's main
class, so ./gradlew run starts a class this project does not have.

Let's name tally.Tally instead, which is what the application plugin
needs in order to run anything, and record the two commands in the
README now that there is a build to describe.

The jar the build produces is still named after the sample project.
A-Jar is where that is dealt with.

commitResults.messageTitle: Build the UI tests through Gradle
commitResults.messageBody:
The test runner calls javac itself, so it compiles the app its own way
rather than the way the build does. That holds only while the app
needs nothing on its classpath; the moment a dependency is declared,
the tests would run a different program from the one that ships.

Let's have the runner ask Gradle to compile and to report the
classpath, then start the app with it. Compiling once and launching
directly keeps the suite near its old speed rather than paying for a
Gradle round trip per case.

Timing the two showed the reason given earlier for calling javac was
wrong: with a warm daemon Gradle compiles in about the same time.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add JUnit tests for the parsing and the tally
commitResults.messageBody:
The only tests are the console ones, which drive the whole chatbot.
They show that a command produces the right reply, but not which
method got a case wrong, and they cannot reach a method that no
command exercises directly.

Let's test the parsing, the task types, the tally and the file with
JUnit. The cases go after the edges rather than the happy path:
numbers just outside the list, dates in the wrong form, an event whose
markers are the wrong way round, a data file with a field too many.

Method names follow the featureUnderTest_testScenario_expectedBehavior
form the coding standard gives for tests.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-JUnit into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Adds unit tests for Parser, the task types, TaskList and Storage, so a
broken method is named by a failing test rather than found by reading
the console output.

commitResults.messageTitle: Package the app as tally.jar
commitResults.messageBody:
The jar the build produces is named after the sample project the build
file came from, so what it hands to a user does not say what it is.

Let's name it tally.jar, and record in the README how to build it and
how to run it, since the point of the jar is that it goes to someone
who does not have this repository.

The jar stays out of the repository, being a generated binary. It
reaches users through a GitHub release instead.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-Jar into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Names the packaged jar after this project, so the single file handed
to a user is recognisable as Tally.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document the packages and the command keyword
commitResults.messageBody:
Every class carries a header comment, but the packages they were sorted
into carry none, so nothing says what belongs in each or why the split
falls where it does. The one public method without a comment is the
command-word getter.

Let's add a package-info for each package, saying what it is for and
naming the classes that carry the weight, and document the getter.
Someone opening the source now meets the shape of the project before
the classes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name a boolean method as a boolean
commitResults.messageBody:
The coding standard asks that a method returning a boolean be named so
it reads as one, with a prefix such as is, has or was. The method
carrying out a command returns whether the conversation should carry
on, but its name says only that it handles something.

Let's call it isStillTalkingAfter, which is what the caller assigns it
to and what the loop condition then reads as.

commitResults.messageTitle: Find tasks by a word in their description
commitResults.messageBody:
A long tally can only be read in full, so a user looking for one task
has to scan every line of it.

Let's accept a "find" command that shows the tasks whose description
contains the word given, matched without regard to case.

Each match keeps the number it has on the whole tally rather than being
numbered among the results. A user who finds a task at 7 can then mark
7, which numbering the matches from 1 would have made wrong.

The list of commands Tally names when it does not recognise one comes
from the enum, so it took in "find" on its own; only the test case
checking that message needed updating.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-JavaDoc into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Adds a package-info for each package and documents the command-word
getter, so the source says what each package is for.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-CodingStandard into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Renames the command-handling method so it reads as the boolean it
returns, as the coding standard asks.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-Level-9 into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Adds the find command, so a task can be located by a word in its
description rather than by reading the whole tally.

commitResults.messageTitle: Record why commands are dispatched by a switch
commitResults.messageBody:
Reading classmates' chatbots shows most give each command a class of
its own with an execute method, the way AddressBook-Level3 does, while
this one switches over an enum. Nothing in the code says the choice was
considered rather than merely arrived at.

Let's say so where the switch is, linking a classmate's pull request as
a worked example of the other approach, and record what would change
the answer: a command needing state of its own, or the risk of adding
an enum constant that nothing carries out, since a switch over an enum
is not checked for exhaustiveness.

commitResults.messageTitle: Check the code style with Checkstyle
commitResults.messageBody:
The Java coding standard is followed by reading it and remembering, so
a violation is only found when someone looks for one. Thirty-three had
accumulated without being noticed.

Let's add the Checkstyle configuration the course provides and wire the
plugin into the build, which puts the checks in Gradle's check task so
a violation fails the build rather than waiting to be spotted. Passing
it is then evidence the standard was followed, not just intended.

The violations it found are fixed: imports of this project's own
packages are separated from the java ones, case labels are indented one
level inside their switch as the standard's own example shows, and a
wrapped argument list opens on the line before. The command switch
gains a default clause, which also turns an unhandled command from
silence into a thrown exception.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-CheckStyle into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Adds the Checkstyle configuration and wires it into the build, so a
coding standard violation now fails the build instead of waiting to be
noticed.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a window for talking to Tally
commitResults.messageBody:
Tally can only be used from a terminal, which rules it out for anyone
who does not have one open, and shows its replies as plain scrolling
text with no sense of a conversation.

Let's add a JavaFX front end: a scrolling conversation of dialog boxes,
a text field, and a picture beside each speaker. The window asks Tally
for a reply as text rather than letting it print, so both front ends
say the same words and cannot drift apart.

Ui gains a mode that records replies instead of printing them, which is
what lets the console keep its horizontal rules while the window leaves
them out; a chat window separates messages by putting each in its own
box. Dialog text is set in a monospace font, without which the banner
and the numbered task list both lose their alignment.

The window is started through a Launcher rather than the Application
subclass itself, because a packaged jar whose main class extends
Application fails with a missing JavaFX runtime error.

JavaFX ships native binaries, so the build works out which artifact to
ask for from the operating system and architecture rather than naming
one, which keeps the jar buildable on any machine.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-Level-10 into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Adds a JavaFX front end, so Tally can be used in a window as well as in
a terminal, with both asking the same chatbot for the same words.

commitResults.messageTitle: Let the conversation scroll
commitResults.messageBody:
Once the conversation grows past the window, everything below the fold
is unreachable: the box holding it is given a fixed height, so it never
grows, and the scroll pane sees content that already fits and offers
nothing to scroll.

Let's let that box take its height from what it holds. The scroll pane
then has something to scroll, and fitting it to the width stops the
messages being narrower than the window.

Scrolling to the newest message is done by watching the height rather
than binding the scroll position to it. A bound property cannot be set,
so binding would have left the user unable to scroll back through what
was said earlier.

commitResults.messageTitle: Follow the tutorial's JavaFX dependencies
commitResults.messageBody:
The build asks for whichever JavaFX binaries suit the machine doing the
building, an approach taken from a classmate's project rather than from
the tutorial. The jar it produces therefore carries Linux binaries
alone, so handing it to anyone on Windows or a Mac gives them an app
that cannot start. A-Jar asks for a jar that runs on someone else's
computer.

Let's declare all three platforms for each module, as the tutorial's
sample does. The jar grows from 8.6M to 12M and now carries binaries
for every platform, which is what makes it worth handing over.

The tutorial also warns that mixing approaches gathered from elsewhere
produces a build that works on one machine and not others. That is
exactly what happened here.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add tasks to the tally several at a time
commitResults.messageBody:
Adding a few tasks means calling add once for each, which is what the
tests do throughout: three calls to say one thing. The two listing
methods also each build their own array of lines, repeating the same
heading-then-numbered-lines arithmetic.

Let's have add take any number of tasks, so adding one reads no
differently from adding several, and let the two listings share the
numbering rather than each doing it by hand.

Varargs suits add because the number of tasks is the only thing that
varies between its uses, and it leaves every existing single-task call
unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-Varargs into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Lets tasks be added several at a time, and shares the numbering the two
listings had each been doing for themselves.

commitResults.messageTitle: Build the saved task list in one expression
commitResults.messageBody:
A test builds the list of tasks it means to save with three separate
add calls, which says one thing in three statements.

Let's build it with List.of, keeping only the task that has to be
marked done before it goes in as a separate step.

commitResults.messageTitle: Clarify names and the dispatch comment
commitResults.messageBody:
Several names describe their values loosely: a list of task positions
is called everything, the varargs parameter added reads as past tense
at the point where nothing has been added yet, and Event's from and to
are prepositions that name nothing. The comment above the command
switch records that AI suggested the construct without saying why it
is built the way it is.

Let's name each value for what it holds, and say inline why the
default clause throws IllegalStateException rather than TallyException.

Event keeps its times as raw strings rather than parsed values, so
start and end are preferred to startTime or startTimeString. Both of
those encode a type the fields may not keep: once events are parsed
the way deadlines already are, such names would have to change at
every use, while start and end would still read correctly. A field
comment carries the raw-text detail instead.

Raised in review on NUS-CS2103-AY2627-S1/ip#30.

commitResults.messageTitle: Rename vague fields and a non-verb method
commitResults.messageBody:
Several names do not say what they hold or do: the StringBuilder
collecting a reply is called pending, Deadline's date is called by,
the lower-cased search term is called wanted, and the method that
builds a numbered listing is called numbered. The coding standard
requires method names to be verbs, so the last of these breaks it
outright. Checkstyle passes it because its MethodName rule validates
the camelCase pattern alone, not the part of speech.

Let's name each one for what it holds or does. The search term becomes
lowercaseWord rather than normalizedWord, because normalized leaves
open how, while lowercase says exactly what was done. Deadline's field
becomes dueDate, which is safe to say here because the field really is
a LocalDate. Storage's matching parameter and the method that drains
the reply buffer take the same words, so one idea reads under one name
throughout.

The /by command word and the "(by: ...)" display text are untouched,
so nothing the user types or sees moves.

Raised in review on NUS-CS2103-AY2627-S1/ip#30.

commitResults.messageTitle: Assert what the parts assume of each other
commitResults.messageBody:
Several assumptions hold only because of the way the parts are wired,
and nothing in the code says so. TaskList.get trusts that its index is
in range, because Parser.parseTaskIndex rejects out-of-range numbers
before returning one. TaskList.add trusts that no task is null,
because Storage.load throws rather than yield one. Tally trusts that
parseCommand never returns null, and Ui.show trusts that it is never
asked to print nothing. A reader has to reconstruct each of these by
hand, and a caller that broke one would fail somewhere else entirely.

Let's state them as assertions, each carrying the reason it should
hold. An assertion suits these better than an exception because they
describe internal wiring rather than user input: what the user types
is already rejected where it arrives, so a failure here means a bug in
the code rather than a mistake at the keyboard.

Assertions are off unless asked for, which would leave every one of
them inert. Gradle enables them for the JUnit tests already, so this
adds -ea to the application's launch arguments and to the console test
runner, which was starting the program without them.

Injecting an off-by-one into parseTaskIndex shows what they buy: an
IndexOutOfBoundsException raised deep inside ArrayList becomes an
AssertionError at TaskList.get naming both the invariant and the
offending index.

commitResults.messageTitle: Give every branch of the switch one level
commitResults.messageBody:
The command switch reads at two altitudes at once. Six of its branches
name an operation and delegate to it, while mark, unmark and delete
each carry three lines of the work inline: look the task up, change
it, say what happened. That pushes the method to 36 lines against a
guideline of 30, and repeats the lookup line verbatim three times.

Let's move those three bodies into methods of their own, so that every
branch is a single call and the switch shows the shape of the
conversation without the detail of any one command. The repeated
lookup becomes taskNamedIn, named for what it yields rather than for
the parsing it does along the way.

The three could instead have folded into one method taking a flag for
which of them to run, which would remove more duplication still. A
boolean at the call site says nothing about its own meaning though,
and the three replies differ regardless, so three named methods read
better here than one parameterised one.

The 24 console cases pass unchanged, which is what shows no behaviour
moved with the code.

commitResults.messageTitle: Build lists with streams rather than loops
commitResults.messageBody:
Five places build a list the same way: declare an empty one, walk a
range or a collection, and add along the way. Whether a given loop
maps, filters, or does both takes a moment's reading to work out,
because the intent is spread over four lines instead of stated in one.

Let's write them as the operations they are. findPositions filters a
range of positions, save maps each task to its line in the file,
Command.parse finds the first constant whose keyword matches,
listKeywords joins the keywords, and showTasks takes every position on
the tally.

Storage.load keeps its loop. It needs the running line number to say
which line of the file defeated it, and it throws from inside the
walk; a stream carrying both would read worse than the loop it
replaced. The increment asks for streams where they apply, and this is
where they do not.

Two of the lists are immutable now, which suits them: no caller ever
changed one, and none can do so by accident from here on.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-Assertions into master
commitResults.messageBody: Documents the assumptions holding between the parts as assertions, each carrying the reason it should hold, and turns assertions on where the app and the console tests run so they are not inert.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-CodeQuality into master
commitResults.messageBody: Brings every branch of the command switch to one level of abstraction, so the switch shows the shape of the conversation without the detail of any single command.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge master into branch-A-Streams
commitResults.messageBody:
Assertions and the reworked command switch have landed on master since
this branch was cut, and formatNumberedTasks was rewritten on both
sides: master put an assertion inside the loop over the positions,
while this branch replaced that loop with a stream.

Keeping either side alone would drop the other, so the assertion moves
ahead of the stream and covers the whole list in one go. It says the
same thing in the form the surrounding code now takes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-Streams into master
commitResults.messageBody:
States five list-building loops as the operations they are, so that
whether one maps, filters or does both reads from the first line
rather than from four. Leaves Storage.load as a loop, since it needs
the running line number to report which line defeated it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Record tasks that may be done within a period
commitResults.messageBody:
Tally knows a task with no date, one with a single date, and one that
runs between two points in time. It has nowhere to put the common case
between them: work that has to happen inside a period, on whichever
day suits. A deadline states only the last acceptable day and says
nothing about when the work may begin.

Let's add a window task, typed as

    window submit form /between 2026-09-08 /and 2026-09-12

Both ends are read as dates rather than kept as text, as a deadline
does and an event does not. That buys two things: the ends print in
the display format Level-8 asks for, and a period running backwards
can be refused where it is typed rather than reaching the tally. Equal
ends are accepted, a window of one day being a period rather than a
mistake.

Deadlines and windows both show dates, so the display formatter moves
up to Task, where one definition serves both and they cannot drift
apart. For the same reason the complaint about an unreadable date no
longer suggests a deadline, since either command can now raise it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-B-DoWithinPeriodTasks into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Adds a fourth kind of task, for work that may be done on any day of a
stated period, so the case between a deadline and an event has
somewhere to go.

commitResults.messageTitle: Find the next stretch of free days
commitResults.messageBody:
The tally can say what is on a day, but not when nothing is. Deciding
when to take on something new means reading the whole list and working
out by hand which days are already spoken for, which is exactly the
sort of counting the program should do.

Let's add a free command, typed as

    free /for 3 /from 2026-09-08

Both markers are optional: bare free offers the next day nothing takes
up, /for asks for that many in a row, and /from moves the search off
today, which also lets the answer be checked against a fixed
expectation rather than one that changes daily.

Each kind of task answers for itself which days it takes up, so the
search asks the tally rather than asking what kind each task is, and a
new kind joins in by overriding one method. A deadline takes its own
day, a window every day of its period, and an event only when its ends
were written as dates. Events keep their ends as typed, so an older
data file still loads and the Level-4 form still works; when one
cannot be read the reply says so, rather than calling a day free on
evidence it does not have.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-B-FindFreeTimes'
Say plainly how far the AI tool was used
commitResults.messageBody:
The acknowledgement names which tool was used and points at the code
it shaped, but leaves how far it went to be inferred from the length
of the list below it. The reuse policy asks for the extent itself, on
the grounds that a reader cannot judge it from examples alone.

Let's state it in the opening sentence, where it is read before the
list rather than reconstructed from it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Stop a failed save destroying what was saved
commitResults.messageBody:
Saving writes straight over the data file, so a write that fails
partway through leaves it truncated mid-line. The tally is then
shorter than it was, one task is cut in half, and nothing on the next
start says so, because whatever remains still parses. A run against a
write limit lost 29 of 61 tasks without a word.

Two things make that worse. Every command saves, list, find and free
included, so a command that changed nothing still rewrites the file
and runs the same risk; on a file it cannot write, each one also
complains. And a second damaged file overwrites the rescue copy of
the first, which is the one case that copy exists for.

Let's write the new tally beside the old one and rename it into
place, so a failed write leaves the old file untouched; save only
after a command that can change the tally, which each Command now
says of itself; and give each rescue copy a free name instead of
replacing the one before it.

Reintroducing any of the three fails a test that now guards it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Keep the tasks a damaged file still holds
commitResults.messageBody:
One line the data file cannot offer as a task costs the user every
other task on it. A file of forty tasks with a single bad line loads
as an empty tally, which is a far worse answer than losing the one
line, and the file is moved away so the rest cannot be recovered from
the app at all.

Let's skip the lines that cannot be read, keep the ones that can, and
say which went. The file is copied rather than moved, because the
tasks that loaded stay on the tally and the next change writes over
the original, which would otherwise take the unreadable lines with
it. Reading now reports rather than fails, so load returns the tasks
together with the note instead of throwing one in place of the other.

A file nobody can read at all is still refused outright: there is
nothing to keep in that case, and nothing to say beyond which file.

This is the behaviour the forum settled on for the same problem after
Level-8 changed how dates are stored, discussed at
NUS-CS2103-AY2627-S1/forum#73.

commitResults.messageTitle: Carry the file's own properties across a save
commitResults.messageBody:
Saving now writes beside the data file and renames the new one over
it, which replaces the file rather than writing into it. Everything
the old file carried is therefore dropped, and three of those matter.

A rename needs permission on the directory rather than on the file,
so a tally the user had protected was overwritten without complaint,
which the plain write it replaced had refused. The new file is made
under the umask, so a tally kept private became readable by others on
the first save. And a data file that was a symbolic link into a
synchronised folder was replaced by an ordinary file, leaving what it
pointed at behind, never to be written again.

Let's follow the link before choosing where to write, refuse a file
the user protected, and give the replacement the permissions its
predecessor had. A half-written file is now cleared where the failure
is caught rather than in a finally, where failing to remove it would
have hidden the reason the save failed.

Copying a damaged file aside also had no limit: reads no longer
rewrite the file, so an unrepaired one was copied again on every
start. It is now copied once, and the reply says so when a copy of
the same damage is already kept.

Each of these fails a test of its own when reverted.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-storage-integrity into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Makes the data file survive the things that were destroying it: a
write that fails partway, a second damaged file, a line that cannot be
read, and the rename that replaces the file on every save.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refuse what the tally cannot carry back
commitResults.messageBody:
Four ways of describing a task are accepted and then cannot be used.

A description holding " | " is written out and read back as a
different number of parts, because the data file separates parts with
it and has no way to escape it. A date written in one of the wider
forms LocalDate reads, such as +999999999-12-31, is accepted and then
overflows the arithmetic the free-day search does on it, which ends
the program. A window running backwards is refused where the user
types one but not where the file offers one, so a file edited by hand
crashes the same search. An event whose two ends are dates the wrong
way round is treated as naming no days at all, and the reply then
says its times are not dates when they plainly are.

Let's refuse the separator where the task is typed, read dates only
in the form the user is told to write, refuse a backwards window from
the file as well as from the user, and read an event's ends the way
they were meant rather than the way they were ordered. Reading a date
in one place rather than two keeps the file and the user held to the
same rule.

Each of the four fails a test of its own when reverted.

commitResults.messageTitle: Ask a task about a day, not for all of them
commitResults.messageBody:
A task was asked to list every day it takes up, which a review showed
does not survive the input it has to survive. An event whose two ends
are dates centuries apart, or written the wrong way round, produces a
list too large to hold, and the program dies of it where it used to
answer. Bounding the years would leave a list of millions.

Let's ask instead whether a task takes up one given day. Nothing is
built to answer it, so ends however far apart cost the same as ends a
day apart, and the search stops holding a set of every day spoken for.
The method also reads as the question it asks, which the list-shaped
one never did.

Two other things the review found. Refusing " | " where the user types
it does not keep a task readable back, because the file joins parts
with a space either side: a description merely ending in a bar builds
the separator when it is saved, and the deadline written that way was
dropped on the next start while the event was silently altered. The
whole character is refused now. And the rule for how a date is written
lived in the parser, out of reach of an event's own ends, which were
the last dates in the program not held to it; it now lives beside the
tasks, where the parser and an event both reach it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Read an event's ends once, and pin the cost
commitResults.messageBody:
An event reads its two ends afresh every time it is asked about a
day, and the free-day search asks every task about every day of a
year. Ten thousand dated events took 1.4 seconds where deadlines,
which hold a date already, took 0.14. Let's read them when the event
is made, since they never change afterwards.

The test meant to hold the memory fix in place did not. Its ends were
outside the form a date may be written in, so they were refused before
anything could be built, and the test passed just as well with the
building put back. It now uses two ordinary dates nine thousand years
apart, which nothing refuses, and asks about a day a thousand times
inside a bound that building even one of those lists would miss.

Refusing every bar is wider than the damage strictly requires: only a
field ending in one, or holding one with a space either side, breaks
the round trip, so "a|b" was safe and is now refused. The narrow rule
was tried first and leaked, and one character with one explanation is
worth more here than a rule that is exactly right and hard to state.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-input-validation into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Refuses the descriptions and dates the tally cannot carry back, holds
the file and the user to one rule for how a date is written, and asks
a task whether it takes up a day rather than for every day it takes
up, which no longer costs what it cannot afford.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name each thing for what it is or does
commitResults.messageBody:
A peer review and two audits found the same handful of names giving
the wrong idea, and most of them are recent enough to have been
written after the review that should have taught the lesson.

Methods have to be verbs, which the coding standard says and
Checkstyle cannot check, since its rule reads the shape of a name
rather than its part of speech. taskNamedIn, countSentence, noteAbout
and refusal are noun phrases sitting among markTask, addTask and
formatNumberedTasks.

Two words are used for two things each. Ui.show prints, while
Task.showDate prints nothing and returns a string, so the latter
becomes formatDate. Storage holds the raw text of a date in fields
named exactly as the parsed LocalDate is named everywhere else, so
those become dueDateText, startDateText and endDateText.

FreeQuery names a LocalDate "from". That is the very fault two peer
reviewers raised on Event and on Deadline, corrected there, and then
written again here in code added afterwards.

The rest name their values loosely: a search phrase called a word
though it holds a phrase and matches within one, a count of free days
called freeInARow, an index called fromMarker, a stream of lines
called numbered, and locals named for what was done to them rather
than what they hold.

commitResults.messageTitle: Say each thing once
commitResults.messageBody:
Four things are written twice or not needed at all.

parseEvent and parseWindow split their arguments on two markers with
nine lines that differ only in the markers, and the reason the order
matters is written beside one of them alone, holding for the other by
accident of the copy. A shared splitter puts that reason in one place.

The greeting is built in getGreeting and again in run, and it is the
one thing the console and the window must not drift apart on, which is
why both already share a Ui. Where the tally is kept is declared in
Tally and again in the window's Main, so the two can come to disagree
about where the user's tasks live; a front end that wants the usual
file now asks Tally for it instead of naming the place itself.

Ui has a constructor nobody calls.

Storage also called two of its methods parseWindow and parseDeadline,
the names Parser uses for methods that throw where these return null.
Reading from a file is not the same as parsing what a user typed, so
they are readWindow and readDeadline now.

commitResults.messageTitle: Let the code say what the numbers meant
commitResults.messageBody:
Reading a task from the file turns on numbers that explain nothing.
Field 1 holds the done flag and field 2 the description, but the code
says only 1 and 2, and a line of each kind is recognised by a length
of 3, 4 or 5 with nothing saying why. The letter each kind is written
under is spelled out twice, once where the task writes itself and
again where Storage reads it back, so the two can come to disagree
about what a D is.

Let's name the positions and the lengths, and let each kind of task
own its letter, so writing and reading and showing all follow one
definition. Changing that letter now moves the file, the display and
the reader together.

The free-day reply was one expression of ten lines holding two
conditionals, computing the same day twice and the same comparison
twice. It is two named methods now, one for a run found and one for
none, leaving the caller to say only which it is.

Also: the window package has no header comment, where every other
package has one, and it is the package a reader knows least; a wrapped
line in TallyTest was indented four spaces rather than eight, which
put it level with the loop body beneath it; and seven test names kept
their expected behaviour but dropped the scenario, which the standard's
three part form asks for.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-code-quality into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Names each thing for what it is or does, says the things that were
said twice once, and lets the code say what the numbers in the data
file meant, following what a peer review and three audits found.

commitResults.messageTitle: Keep each method to one job and one level
commitResults.messageBody:
Two methods had grown past the thirty lines the guideline asks about,
both of them by the fixes made to them this week: the dispatcher took
on deciding when to save, and reading the file took on collecting the
lines it could not read. Let's give the dispatcher's switch a method
of its own, leave the caller to say only whether the conversation goes
on, and lift the file reading out of the method that makes sense of
what was read.

The switch also asked its branches for three different things. Some
were handed a value already worked out, some were handed the raw
arguments and left to work it out themselves, and one was handed
nothing. Every branch now parses at the dispatch and passes down what
it got, so the switch reads as the list of commands it is.

Ending the conversation is decided before the switch rather than
inside it, which is where the reader looks for it, and leaves the rest
of the method to the commands that carry on.

Reading what follows a marker was written out by hand twice in
parseFreeQuery, a level below everything around it. It has a name now.

commitResults.messageTitle: Act on what the final review found
commitResults.messageBody:
Two faults were real, and the rest is what four audits and a separate
review turned up in one sweep. They interleave within the same files,
so they are one commit rather than the six they should be.

- free finds its markers with indexOf and startsWith, so a word that
  merely begins with one is taken for it: "/forgotten" is read as a
  /for, and "/from 2026-09-08 /for 3" hands the whole rest of the line
  to the date reader, which complains about a date the user wrote
  correctly. The arguments are read as words now and each marker
  matched whole; either order is accepted, since both are optional and
  neither is ambiguous, while a repeated or unknown one is refused.
- Window says its end is never before its start and lets any caller
  build one that is, after which it quietly takes up no days at all.
  The parser and the storage reader both refuse one, so an assertion
  says who is at fault when one arrives anyway.
- The fields of a task are protected without a subclass touching any
  of them; they are private now.
- Three comments describe behaviour the code no longer has: loading
  throws on a bad line, copying aside moves the file, and a switch
  sits in the method whose comment explains it. A fourth documents a
  constant deleted two commits ago, and miscounts the commands.
- The done flag and the field separator are named in one place and
  written out as literals in five others.
- Eleven checkstyle modules carry severity=warning, which Gradle lets
  through by default, so the build did not fail on a violation of any
  of them. It does now.

commitResults.messageTitle: Repair the comments a rename damaged
commitResults.messageBody:
Renaming unreadable to unreadableLines was done by pattern over whole
files, so it rewrote the prose as well as the code: a comment now
reads "take the unreadableLines lines with it", and another says a
date "is unreadableLines". Renaming is only mechanical inside code.

Several other comments describe a program that has moved on. The
storage package says a damaged file is moved aside, when it is copied
and only the unreadable lines are dropped. The task package lists
three kinds of task, and there are four. The ui package describes
printing to a terminal alone, though the same class now gathers words
for a window instead. Tally calls itself a command-line chatbot. The
example line for a deadline shows a date as "June 6th", which is not
a form the file has ever held.

Two names in Storage claim more than they hold. The two indices after
the description are called dates, but an event keeps whatever the
user typed there, and isWellFormed checks only the parts every task
shares while the parts belonging to each kind are checked afterwards.

Saving also did seven things in one method: made the folder, followed
a link, refused a protected file, named and wrote a temporary one,
carried permissions across, put it in place and cleared up after
itself. Deciding where to write and writing the replacement are their
own methods now, leaving save to say only what happens in what order.

commitResults.messageTitle: Say what a method does, and hold what cannot change
commitResults.messageBody:
isStillTalkingAfter reads as a question about a line. It parses the
line, carries the command out, changes the tally, prints the reply and
saves the file, and the answer it returns is the smallest thing it
does. A name beginning with is promises otherwise, so it is runCommand
now, with the answer stated in its documentation.

The window's input handler read the box, asked Tally, built two
bubbles, cleared the box, disabled the controls, timed an animation
and closed the program. Showing a turn and arranging to leave are
their own methods now.

Ui keeps no scanner when it is answering a window, and the three
methods that read from one said nothing about it: a front end that
called them met a null with nothing to say for itself. They refuse the
call and say why. Ui also gathered every reply into a buffer nobody
reads on the console, growing for the life of the session; it gathers
them only when something is waiting to collect them.

What is set once and never again now says so: the tally, the note
about the data file, a task's description, and the format dates are
shown in, which no subclass reaches for since they all call formatDate.
The note is an Optional rather than a field that may be null, which is
what the reader already hands over.

commitResults.messageTitle: Stop losing a tally nobody could read
commitResults.messageBody:
A data file that is there but cannot be read leaves Tally starting
empty, and the copy meant to rescue it fails for the same reason. The
file is still writable, so the first command the user types writes an
empty tally straight over contents nobody has seen. Refusing to write
until the file can be read is the only answer that keeps them.

A command changes the tally before it can be saved, so a save that
fails left the user told it worked, looking at a list a restart would
take away. The file is read back when a save fails, and the tally put
back the way the file has it, so what is shown is what would come
back. When even that read fails the reply says so rather than
implying the change is kept.

Three smaller ways the file was mishandled. A line with the right
number of parts but a blank one among them was loaded as a task, so a
deadline with no description sat on the tally as a nameless entry.
Saving wrote a temporary file at a fixed name beside the data file,
which would overwrite whatever already had that name and would collide
with a second Tally saving at once; it takes a name of its own now.
And the search folded case in the machine's own language, which turns
an I into a dotless one in Turkish.

commitResults.messageTitle: Say what each class and comment actually means
commitResults.messageBody:
Task is concrete, but the line it writes is only the part every kind
of task shares, so a plain Task could never be written as something
the reader would take back. It is abstract now, which says so.

Parser holds nothing and is all static, yet could be instantiated.
Command.listKeywords is public though only the parser's own message
ever wants it.

The rest is comments that no longer describe the program. Another two
were damaged by the same rename as before, one reading "the line
lineNumbers". parseDate is documented as reading what follows /by,
though every command taking a date now goes through it. asList
promises that changing the list cannot change the tally, when the
tasks in it are the same objects and marking one through the list
marks it on the tally. Ui.show says it prints, though for a window it
prints nothing and gathers the words instead. The package comment
still calls Tally command-line only.
